questions.q: How does a general graph differ from a tree?
questions.explain: A graph is just vertices and edges. A tree is a special graph: connected, no cycles, one root, and exactly n − 1 edges. Graphs drop all of those rules, which is why walking them needs more care.
options: A graph cannot have weights on its edges
A graph has no root and no "one parent" rule, and it may contain cycles
A graph always has more vertices than edges

questions.q: Which relationship should be modelled with directed edges?
questions.explain: "A uses B" does not imply "B uses A", so the edge has a direction. Mutual friendship, two-way roads and "bought together" are symmetric, so undirected edges fit.
options: Two people are friends on a network where friendship is mutual
Two cities are connected by a two-way road
Two products are often bought together

questions.q: A rider-routing app asks for the fastest route. What should the edge weights be?
questions.explain: The algorithm optimises whatever the weights mean. Distance gives the shortest route, not the fastest; a short road through a busy market can be slower. Travel times change, so they must be updatable.
options: Expected travel time on that stretch, updated as traffic changes
The number of junctions on the road

questions.q: A city map is stored as an undirected graph. What bug does that cause?
questions.explain: An undirected edge can be used in both directions. One-way streets need a directed edge; a two-way street becomes two directed edges, one each way.
options: Routes will be longer than necessary
Riders can be sent the wrong way down one-way streets
Nothing, as long as the weights are correct

questions.q: In a directed "follows" graph, what does the in-degree of a person count?
questions.explain: In-degree counts edges arriving at a vertex; an edge A → B means A follows B, so arrows into B are B's followers. Out-degree counts the people B follows.
options: How many mutual follows they have
The length of the longest path from them

questions.q: A delivery map has 100,000 junctions and about 250,000 road segments. Which representation fits, and why?
questions.explain: A matrix always uses V² cells. With 100,000 vertices that is 10¹⁰ cells for a few hundred thousand edges. An adjacency list uses O(V + E) memory and lists a junction's roads in O(degree).
options: An adjacency matrix, because edge checks are O(1)
An adjacency list, because the graph is sparse and a matrix would need 10 billion mostly empty cells
An edge list sorted by weight
Either; they use the same memory

questions.q: When is an adjacency matrix a good choice?
questions.explain: The matrix answers "edge a → b?" with one array access, but costs O(V²) memory and O(V) to list neighbours. That trade only pays off when V is small or the graph is dense.
options: For road networks with millions of junctions
For small or dense graphs where you mostly ask "is there an edge between a and b?"

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Three undirected roads are stored twice each, once from each end: 6 entries across 4 cities. Because the reverse entry exists, Benin → Lagos finds 312.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The repeated follow adds nothing to a Set, so Ada follows 1 person. Finding Tunde's followers requires scanning everyone's list (O(V + E)), because edges are only stored in the "follows" direction. Chioma does not follow Ada.

questions.q: Your app asks "who follows X?" on every profile view. What is the usual fix?
questions.explain: Storing both directions doubles the memory but makes both questions O(degree). An undirected graph would lose the difference between following and being followed.
options: Scan every user's follow list each time
Keep a second, reversed adjacency list, updated on every follow and unfollow
Store follows in an adjacency matrix

questions.q: Why does every graph walk need a visited set, when a tree walk does not?
questions.explain: A tree has exactly one path to each node. In a graph, shared dependencies create many paths (the number can double at every layer) and a cycle creates infinitely many.
options: Graphs are always bigger than trees
A vertex can be reached by several paths, and cycles lead back to where you started; without memory you repeat work or loop forever

questions.q: How many visits does a walk without a visited set make here?
questions.explain: There are two paths to db (through auth and through orders), so db and both of its dependencies are visited twice: api, auth, orders, db ×2, config ×2, logger ×2 = 9. With a visited set it would be 6, and the gap doubles with each extra "diamond".

questions.q: With a visited set, what does finding everything reachable from one vertex cost?
questions.explain: Each vertex is pushed at most once and each edge is examined at most once (from its source vertex). That is linear in the size of the graph.

questions.q: What is a topological order of a directed graph?
questions.explain: It is an order that respects every edge. For dependencies, with edges from a dependency to the packages that need it, it is a valid build order.
options: An order of all vertices where, for every edge u → v, u comes before v
The order a breadth-first search visits them

questions.q: When does a topological order exist?
questions.explain: On a cycle, each vertex must come before the next one, all the way round, which is impossible. Without cycles, Kahn's algorithm always succeeds.
options: Only when the graph is a tree
Exactly when the directed graph has no cycles
Only when every vertex has in-degree at most 1

questions.q: config, logger and money have no dependencies and nothing relates them. What does that mean for the build order?
questions.explain: Topological order is usually not unique. Any order of unrelated packages is correct, but a build that changes order between machines can hide order-dependent bugs, so tie-breaking should be fixed (declaration order or sorted names).
options: The graph has no topological order
Several orders are valid; tools make the choice deterministic so every machine builds the same way

questions.q: A developer runs Kahn's algorithm directly on the "uses" edges (api → auth, auth → db). What comes out?
questions.explain: Kahn's algorithm puts every edge's source first. With "uses" edges, the package that uses things comes first, which is backwards for building. Either reverse the edges ("is needed by") or reverse the result.
options: The build order exactly reversed: api first, db last
An error, because the graph has a cycle

questions.q: What does this Kahn's algorithm print? (Edges point from a dependency to the packages that need it.)
questions.explain: config and money start with in-degree 0. Processing config lowers auth to 1 and db to 0, so db joins the queue after money. Then users, and only after users is auth free (its in-degree reaches 0).

questions.q: The data has a cycle. What does this print?
questions.explain: db and users wait for each other, so neither reaches in-degree 0. orders is not on the cycle, but it depends on users, so it is blocked too. Kahn's algorithm reports everything blocked; finding the actual loop (db ↔ users) needs the depth-first version.

questions.q: What is the cost of Kahn's algorithm, and why?
questions.explain: Computing in-degrees looks at every edge once, and so does processing the queue. Rescanning all packages each round, as the naive version at the start does, is what makes that one slower.
options: O(V²), because it scans for ready vertices each round
O(V + E): each vertex enters the queue once and each edge is followed once
O(E log V), because it uses a priority queue

questions.q: Packages in the same stage can be built in parallel. What does this print?
questions.explain: Stage 1 is everything with no dependencies. Processing config frees cache (it only needs config); processing logger then frees db (it needed both). So stage 2 is cache and db. api needs both, so it waits for stage 3. Three stages is the length of the longest chain.

questions.q: A monorepo's longest dependency chain has 6 packages, and there are 40 packages in total. Each build takes 2 minutes. With unlimited parallel workers, what is the fastest possible full build?
questions.explain: Packages on a chain must be built one after another, so the longest chain (the critical path) sets the minimum: 6 × 2 = 12 minutes. More workers help with wide stages but can never shorten the chain.
options: It depends only on the number of workers

questions.q: The depth-first topological sort marks vertices as "in progress" while their dependencies are being visited. Why not just "visited" or "not visited"?
questions.explain: With only "visited", you cannot tell a cycle (the vertex is on the current path) from a diamond (the vertex was finished earlier through another path). The in-progress state is exactly the current path, which is also the cycle you report.
options: Reaching an in-progress vertex means you went round a loop; reaching a done vertex is just a shared dependency, which is fine

questions.q: What does this depth-first topological sort print?
questions.explain: A package is added only after everything it uses: post-order. Visiting api goes to orders, then db, then config (added first), then db, orders; auth finds db and config done and is added; api is last. (This version has no cycle detection; the lesson's adds the in-progress state.)

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When db tries to visit auth, auth is still active, so the path from auth to the current vertex is the loop. api is on the path but not on the loop, which is why the slice starts at auth.

questions.q: A package lists @shop/userz (a typo) as a dependency. What should a dependency resolver do?
questions.explain: Silently inventing a vertex hides the typo, and the real dependency is then missing from the order. Checking names against the known set turns a confusing build failure into a clear message.
options: Add @shop/userz as a new package with no dependencies
Report it as unknown, so the typo (or an external dependency) is visible
Remove the package that lists it

questions.q: A package lists itself as a dependency. What should Kahn's algorithm report?
questions.explain: The self-edge gives it in-degree 1, and only the package itself could lower that. It never enters the queue, so it appears in blocked, as the lesson's test checks.
options: It is blocked: a self-edge is a cycle of length one, so its in-degree never reaches 0
It goes first, because it depends only on itself

questions.q: Why does the lesson iterate packages in declaration order (a Map keeps insertion order) instead of, say, the order a Set of strings was filled from a network response?
questions.explain: Any valid order is correct, but a build that orders things differently from run to run makes order-dependent bugs appear and vanish. A fixed tie-break makes builds reproducible.
options: So the same input always produces the same order on every machine and every run
Because topological sort requires alphabetical input
Because Maps cannot hold package names

questions.q: The test generates random DAGs by shuffling vertices and only adding edges from earlier to later positions. Why can that never create a cycle?
questions.explain: A cycle would need at least one edge going backwards. The shuffled order is itself a topological order of the graph, by construction.
options: Every edge goes forwards in the shuffled order, so no path can come back to an earlier vertex
Because each vertex has at most one edge

questions.q: Which property check proves an output is a valid topological order?
questions.explain: That is the definition, checked directly: completeness (every vertex, once) plus order (every edge forwards). The other checks can pass for wrong outputs.
options: Every vertex appears exactly once, and for every edge u → v, u's position is before v's
The output has the same length as the input

questions.q: Each lesson's week is one more than its latest prerequisite's week. Processing in topological order, what does this print?
questions.explain: The keys happen to be listed in a topological order, so each lesson's prerequisites already have weeks. Recursion and hash maps can share week 2, graphs and heaps can share week 4. The largest value, 4, is the length of the longest chain.
options: javascript:1 recursion:2 hash maps:2 trees:3 graphs:4 heaps:4
javascript:1 recursion:2 hash maps:3 trees:4 graphs:5 heaps:6
javascript:1 recursion:2 hash maps:2 trees:3 graphs:4 heaps:5
javascript:0 recursion:1 hash maps:1 trees:2 graphs:3 heaps:3

questions.q: An application registers components with dependencies (the database depends on config, the HTTP server on the database). In which order should they stop at shutdown?
questions.explain: A component must stop before the things it depends on, so it never uses a closed database. That is the startup topological order reversed, which is what reverseTopologicalSort in @zudojs/lifecycle returns.
options: The reverse of the startup order: the HTTP server first, config last

questions.q: Finish addEdge(graph, from, to, weight) for an adjacency list stored as a Map of Maps. If directed is false, store the edge both ways. It should print Lagos:Ibadan,Benin Ibadan:Lagos Benin:Lagos | Ada:Tunde Tunde:.
questions.explain: Create both vertices if they are missing (so Tunde exists even with no outgoing edges), then store the edge, and the reverse edge only for undirected graphs.

questions.q: Finish tripLength(roads, stops): add up the km for each consecutive pair of stops, and throw no road from A to B if a leg does not exist. It should print 568 and then no road from Ibadan to Kano.
questions.explain: Each leg is an O(1) average lookup, so checking a trip of k stops is O(k). ?. handles a start city that does not exist at all, and comparing with undefined (not a truthiness check) would still work for a road of length 0.
questions.expected:
568
no road from Ibadan to Kano

questions.q: Finish transitiveDeps(uses, start): return every package reachable from start (not including it), visiting each package once. Use an explicit stack and a visited set. The program sorts the result, so it should print auth, catalog, config, db, logger, money, orders, users.
questions.explain: Mark a package as seen when you push it, so it is never pushed twice even when several packages use it. invoices is not reachable from api, so it is not included. O(V + E).
questions.expected: auth, catalog, config, db, logger, money, orders, users

questions.q: Finish buildOrder(uses) with Kahn's algorithm. uses maps a package to the packages it uses. Return { order, blocked }. First reverse the edges so they point from a dependency to the packages that need it. It should print the two lines shown.
questions.explain: A package's in-degree is the number of packages it uses; it is ready at 0. Building a package lowers the count of everything that needs it. In the broken input, auth and db wait for each other, and api waits for auth, so all three are blocked.
questions.expected:
db money auth api | blocked:
money | blocked: api auth db

questions.q: Finish findCycle(uses): return the first dependency loop found as an array like ["users", "db", "users"], or null if there is none. Use depth-first search with three states. It should print null and then auth -> users -> db -> auth.
questions.explain: "active" means on the current path. Meeting an active vertex again closes a loop, and the path from that vertex onwards is the loop itself. "done" vertices were fully explored without finding a loop, so they are skipped. O(V + E).

questions.q: Finish mutualFollows(follows, person): return the people that person follows who also follow them back. follows maps each user to a Set of the users they follow. It should print Tunde, Emeka.
questions.explain: For each outgoing edge, check the reverse edge with an O(1) Set lookup: O(out-degree) in total. Chioma is followed by Ada but does not follow her back.

questions.q: Finish affected(uses, changed): return every package that directly or indirectly uses changed, so CI knows what to retest. Reverse the graph first, then walk it. It should print api, catalog, invoices, orders.
questions.explain: "Who is affected by money?" follows the edges backwards, so build the reversed graph (O(V + E)) and walk it with a visited set (O(V + E)). auth and users do not touch money and can skip their tests.

questions.q: Both loops list the neighbours of one city. How many cells or entries does each look at?
questions.explain: Same answer, very different cost. The matrix must check every cell in the row, O(V), even though city 0 has only three roads. The list holds only the neighbours, O(degree).

questions.q: Roads are one-way (directed). Which cities can a rider reach from each starting point?
questions.explain: From Lagos: Ibadan, Ilorin, Abuja (and back to Lagos, which is already seen). Abuja has no outgoing roads. Kano reaches only Abuja. The cycle is harmless because of the visited set; in a directed graph, reachability is not symmetric.
options: It never finishes, because Lagos, Ibadan and Ilorin form a cycle

questions.q: Startup stages are reversed to get the shutdown order, and each stage is reversed too. What does this print?
questions.explain: The stage list is reversed so dependents stop before their dependencies, and each stage is reversed so the shutdown mirrors startup exactly. Spreading into new arrays first leaves startup unchanged; calling startup.reverse() directly would have mutated it.
options:
http+queue then database then cache+logger then config
config

queue+http then database then logger+cache then config
config

http+queue then database then cache+logger then config
http

config then logger+cache then database then queue+http
